↑ Back to F17

F17:1 Automated RAG Evals Harness: Turning "Did That Change Help or Hurt?" Into a Number

Every feature built so far — Cross-Encoder Re-ranking (F10), LangGraph State Machine Engine (F13), and every prompt tweak to RAG System Prompt & Persona (F3.1) along the way — was verified the same way: ask it a real question, read the answer, decide by eye whether it's still good. That works for one change reviewed by the person who made it. It doesn't scale past that, and it can't catch a regression nobody thought to manually re-check — a re-ranking model swap that quietly favors the wrong chunk type, a prompt edit that reads fine but drifts the model toward inventing details, a hybrid-search weighting (Hybrid Search (F18)) that trades recall for precision in a way that only shows up on the questions nobody re-tested by hand.

Automated RAG Evals Harness replaces "read it and decide" with a fixed, repeatable suite: 15 known questions (5 per cuisine) with known-good answers, run through the exact same get_engine(...).answer(...) call path production traffic hits, scored against three RAG-specific metrics instead of a person's impression. The output is a per-question pass/fail plus an overall count (e.g. 4/5 passed) — the same shape as a test suite's exit code, which is exactly the point: CI/CD Eval Regression Gate (F20) can gate a pull request on it the same way it already gates on pytest failing.

The Big Picture: How the Harness Is Structured

Three pieces, run in sequence by one script:

  • ground-truth dataset (evaluation/fixtures/*.json): a fixed set of 5 test questions per cuisine, each paired with a known-good answer sourced straight from that cuisine's actual menu PDF (real prices, hours, and policy text — not placeholder copy) — checked into the repo like fixture data, not regenerated per run, so a score change means the system changed, not the test
  • the run itself (evaluation/run_evals.py): every question goes through engines.base.get_engine(...) — Modular Engine Strategy Factory (F12)'s same factory production code calls — so the harness is testing the real answering path, not a parallel test-only shortcut that could drift from what users actually hit
  • scoring (evaluation/scoring.py): each answer graded on three axes — faithfulness (is anything in the answer not actually supported by the retrieved context — the automated version of RAG System Prompt & Persona (F3.1)'s "never invent" instruction), answer relevancy (does the answer actually address what was asked), and context precision (did retrieval hand back chunks that were actually useful) — then rolled up into one pass/fail per question against a defined threshold

What's Imported (and Why)

  • pydantic.BaseModel / Field — MetricJudgment's schema (a score plus a reasoning string), passed to llm.with_structured_output(...) so each metric call comes back as a typed score instead of free text to parse — see the toolbox below for why this replaces ragas/deepeval rather than wrapping them
  • core.llm.build_llm_and_embeddings — the same provider selection every engine uses (F2/F12), reused here to build the judge LLM; the harness never hand-rolls its own OpenAI/Azure client
  • engines.base.get_engine — the same F12 factory every real request goes through, so the harness never duplicates engine-selection or retrieval logic that could drift from production behavior
  • a small ground-truth loader (plain JSON, no new dependency) — question/expected-answer pairs per cuisine, kept as static fixture data alongside the harness rather than generated at run time

For the full, step-by-step code implementation, class structures, and technical configuration, please refer to the GitHub Repository & Code Details link.

Tags: Evals, LLM-as-Judge, RAG Evaluation, F17

Tools & Libraries (per checklist.csv's "Primary Tools & Libraries" for #17):
  • Ragas / DeepEval — not used. Both implement exactly these three metrics, which is why the checklist names them — but installing either into this repo's venv backtracks hard on the pinned versions every other engine depends on: pip install ragas --dry-run here resolves to downgrading openai 3.3.1 → 1.109.1 and langchain-openai 1.6.0 → 1.1.9 (confirmed before deciding against it, not assumed) — a downgrade that would break core/llm.py's provider selection and every engine built on it (Modular Engine Strategy Factory (F12), LangGraph State Machine Engine (F13)) just to add an eval script. evaluation/scoring.py implements the same three metrics as direct LLM-judge calls instead — see F17:6.
  • Structured output (with_structured_output) — used, not called out in the checklist by name, but it's what makes each metric call return a typed MetricJudgment (score + reasoning) instead of a score parsed out of free text — the same pattern LangGraph State Machine Engine (F13)'s RouteDecision/VerifyDecision route/verify nodes already established.

F17:2 Architecture Summary: Three Files, One New Judge-Call Pattern

No production code changed to make this possible — engines.base.get_engine(...) (F12) already returns something with the answer(cuisine, question, session_id, use_memory) contract the harness needs, and core.llm.build_llm_and_embeddings() (F2/F12) already returns an LLM the harness can reuse as its judge. The suite's only structural pieces:

  • evaluation/ground_truth.py — a two-item loader: CUISINES (the same three cuisines engines/plain_rag_engine.py's AVAILABLE_CUISINES lists) and load_ground_truth(cuisine), which reads evaluation/fixtures/<cuisine>.json — a plain list of {"question", "expected_answer"} pairs.
  • evaluation/scoring.py — three prompt templates (FAITHFULNESS_PROMPT, ANSWER_RELEVANCY_PROMPT, CONTEXT_PRECISION_PROMPT), one MetricJudgment each returns via llm.with_structured_output(MetricJudgment), and score_answer(llm, question, answer, context), which runs all three and returns them as a tuple. EvalScore wraps one scored question and exposes .passed — true only if all three scores clear their threshold (FAITHFULNESS_THRESHOLD/ANSWER_RELEVANCY_THRESHOLD = 0.8, CONTEXT_PRECISION_THRESHOLD = 0.6).
  • evaluation/run_evals.py — the entrypoint: for every cuisine and every fixture question, calls get_engine(engine_name).answer(cuisine, question, session_id, use_memory=False) (F12's factory), joins the returned source_documents into one context string, scores it via evaluation/scoring.py, then report() prints a per-question pass/fail breakdown (reasoning shown only for failures) and returns whether every question passed. main() exits non-zero if not — the hook CI/CD Eval Regression Gate (F20) is meant to build a build-time gate on top of.

Two Entrypoints, What Each One Actually Pulls In

Only two commands ever get run directly (see F17:4 for the full instructions) — everything else below them is imported transitively, never invoked by hand:

  • python -m evaluation.run_evals — live, needs OPENAI_API_KEY/AZURE_OPENAI_API_KEY
    • core.llm.build_llm_and_embeddings — same provider selection every engine uses
      • langchain_openai (ChatOpenAI/AzureChatOpenAI, OpenAIEmbeddings/AzureOpenAIEmbeddings)
    • engines.base.get_engine — F12's factory
      • engines.plain_rag_engine.PlainRagEngine — lazy-imported only for --engine plain_rag (the default)
        • core.llm.build_llm_and_embeddings (same call, shared)
        • core.memory.wrap_with_memory
        • core.vectorstore.get_retriever
          • flashrank.Ranker — the cross-encoder re-ranking model (F10) — see F17:8 for the cache-directory bug this surfaced
          • langchain_community.vectorstores.FAISS
          • langchain_community.document_loaders.PyPDFLoader — only if vectorstores/<cuisine>/ isn't already cached on disk
      • engines.langgraph_engine.LangGraphEngine — same shape instead, only for --engine langgraph
    • evaluation.ground_truth (CUISINES, load_ground_truth) — reads evaluation/fixtures/<cuisine>.json (a file read, not an import)
    • evaluation.scoring (EvalScore, score_answer)
      • pydantic (BaseModel, Field)
  • pytest tests/test_evaluation.py -v — offline, no API key, no network
    • unittest.mock.MagicMock — stands in for the LLM entirely
    • evaluation.ground_truth — the real fixture files are read (fixture data isn't mocked, only the judge is)
    • evaluation.scoring — the real scoring logic runs, just fed a fake LLM

The pytest path never imports core.llm, engines.base, flashrank, FAISS, or an OpenAI client at all — those modules simply never get loaded, since test_evaluation.py only imports evaluation.ground_truth and evaluation.scoring and mocks the LLM they'd otherwise call. That's also why it's the fast, offline path and run_evals is the one that needs a live provider and hit the F17:8 cache bug in the first place.

F17:3 Integration Guide: What Actually Got Touched

  • evaluation/ (new directory) — __init__.py, ground_truth.py, scoring.py, run_evals.py, and fixtures/sushi.json / steak.json / italian.json (5 questions each, sourced from the actual menu PDFs' prices, hours, and policies).
  • tests/test_evaluation.py (new) — unit tests for the scoring/loading logic, with the LLM judge mocked out (see F17:4).
  • requirements.txt — unchanged. No new dependency: the harness reuses core.llm, engines.base, and pydantic, all already installed for other engines — see F17:2's toolbox for why ragas/deepeval specifically weren't added.
  • engines/base.py, engines/plain_rag_engine.py, core/llm.py — read, not modified. The harness calls get_engine(...) exactly like engine_api.py does; nothing about the answering path needed to change to become testable.

F17:4 Testing Guide: How to run Automated RAG Evals Harness (F17)

1) Offline unit tests — the scoring/loading logic, with the LLM judge mocked out (same shape as Unit Tests for Core Modules (F23)'s suite): no .env, no API key, no network.

source venv/bin/activate
pytest tests/test_evaluation.py -v

2) The real eval run — this one is not offline: every fixture question goes through a real get_engine("plain_rag").answer(...) call (an embeddings + chat completion round trip) and then three more chat completion calls to the judge LLM, so it needs the same OPENAI_API_KEY/AZURE_OPENAI_API_KEY in the repo-root .env every other engine uses:

source venv/bin/activate
python -m evaluation.run_evals

Runs all 15 fixture questions (5 per cuisine) against the plain_rag engine. Narrower runs while iterating:

python -m evaluation.run_evals --cuisine sushi                  # one cuisine
python -m evaluation.run_evals --cuisine sushi --cuisine steak  # repeatable flag
python -m evaluation.run_evals --engine langgraph                # score F13's graph engine instead

Exit code is 0 if every question passed, 1 otherwise — the signal CI/CD Eval Regression Gate (F20) is meant to build a build-time gate on top of.

3) What a real run actually looks like — python -m evaluation.run_evals --cuisine sushi against the live plain_rag engine and the real sushi menu:

[PASS] What's in the Dragon Roll and how much does it cost?
    faithfulness=1.00  answer_relevancy=1.00  context_precision=0.80
[PASS] What are your hours on Friday?
    faithfulness=1.00  answer_relevancy=1.00  context_precision=1.00
[PASS] Is there a corkage fee if I bring my own wine?
    faithfulness=1.00  answer_relevancy=1.00  context_precision=0.80
[FAIL] What vegan options do you have?
    faithfulness=1.00  answer_relevancy=1.00  context_precision=0.50
      context_precision: Out of the retrieved chunks, two are clearly vegan options (Sea Salt Edamame and
      Spicy Garlic Edamame), while the others are either vegetarian or contain non-vegan ingredients, making
      the overall relevance mixed.
[PASS] How much is valet parking?
    faithfulness=1.00  answer_relevancy=1.00  context_precision=1.00

4/5 passed
Verification: run live against all three cuisines' real menus (15 questions total, no mocking) — faithfulness and answer_relevancy scored 1.00 on every single question (RAG System Prompt & Persona (F3.1)'s "never invent" instruction and Cross-Encoder Re-ranking (F10) are doing their job), but context_precision failed 4 of 15, and every failure is the same shape: a narrow single-fact question ("do you accept cash?", "do you deliver?", "what vegan options do you have?") against a restaurant whose FAISS index chunked the entire "RESTAURANT INFORMATION & POLICIES" bullet list into one or two ~500-character chunks (Test the chunking (RAG & Vectorstore) (F3)'s chunk_size=500). Retrieval correctly returns the one chunk with the answer in it — but that chunk also contains four or five unrelated policies, so the judge marks half the retrieved context as noise even though the answer itself is perfect. This is exactly the chunk-size/relevance trade-off F3's own "Interview angle" box already named as something to validate empirically against Context Precision rather than assume forever — F17 is now the thing that actually measures it, and the first real run already turned up a concrete case for it.

# F17: Automated RAG Evals Harness - runs every ground-truth question through the same
# engines.base.get_engine(...) production factory Modular Engine Strategy Factory (F12) uses,
# scores each answer against faithfulness/answer_relevancy/context_precision (evaluation/scoring.py),
# and reports a single pass/fail number - the same shape as a pytest exit code, so CI/CD Eval
# Regression Gate (F20) can gate a pull request on it the same way it already gates on `pytest`
# failing.
#
# Usage:
#   python -m evaluation.run_evals
#   python -m evaluation.run_evals --cuisine sushi
#   python -m evaluation.run_evals --engine langgraph
import argparse
import sys
import uuid

from dotenv import find_dotenv, load_dotenv

from core.llm import build_llm_and_embeddings  # F2/F12: same provider selection as every engine
from engines.base import get_engine  # F12
from evaluation.ground_truth import CUISINES, load_ground_truth
from evaluation.scoring import EvalScore, score_answer

load_dotenv(find_dotenv())


def run(engine_name: str, cuisines: list[str]) -> list[EvalScore]:
    engine = get_engine(engine_name)  # F12: the same factory production traffic hits
    judge_llm, _ = build_llm_and_embeddings()  # a separate LLM call from the answering engine's own, so the judge never grades its own homework's raw client state
    session_id = f"eval-{uuid.uuid4()}"  # one throwaway session per run

    results = []
    for cuisine in cuisines:
        for case in load_ground_truth(cuisine):
            # use_memory=False: each fixture question is graded independently - conversation
            # memory carrying over between unrelated fixture questions would make a score change
            # mean "the memory state drifted", not "the system changed" (see evaluation/ground_truth.py).
            response = engine.answer(cuisine, case["question"], session_id, use_memory=False)
            answer = response["result"]
            context = "\n\n".join(doc.page_content for doc in response["source_documents"])

            faithfulness, answer_relevancy, context_precision = score_answer(
                judge_llm, case["question"], answer, context
            )
            results.append(EvalScore(
                question=case["question"],
                answer=answer,
                faithfulness=faithfulness,
                answer_relevancy=answer_relevancy,
                context_precision=context_precision,
            ))
    return results


def report(results: list[EvalScore]) -> bool:
    """Prints a per-question breakdown (reasoning only for failures) and the pass/fail summary
    line CI/CD Eval Regression Gate (F20) is meant to key off of. Returns True iff every
    question passed."""
    for r in results:
        status = "PASS" if r.passed else "FAIL"
        print(f"[{status}] {r.question}")
        print(
            f"    faithfulness={r.faithfulness.score:.2f}  "
            f"answer_relevancy={r.answer_relevancy.score:.2f}  "
            f"context_precision={r.context_precision.score:.2f}"
        )
        if not r.passed:
            for name, judgment in (
                ("faithfulness", r.faithfulness),
                ("answer_relevancy", r.answer_relevancy),
                ("context_precision", r.context_precision),
            ):
                print(f"      {name}: {judgment.reasoning}")

    passed = sum(1 for r in results if r.passed)
    print(f"\n{passed}/{len(results)} passed")
    return passed == len(results)


def main():
    parser = argparse.ArgumentParser(description="F17: run the RAG eval suite against the checked-in ground-truth fixtures.")
    parser.add_argument("--engine", default="plain_rag", choices=["plain_rag", "langgraph"])
    parser.add_argument(
        "--cuisine", action="append", dest="cuisines", choices=CUISINES,
        help="repeatable (e.g. --cuisine sushi --cuisine steak); defaults to all cuisines",
    )
    args = parser.parse_args()

    results = run(args.engine, args.cuisines or CUISINES)
    all_passed = report(results)
    sys.exit(0 if all_passed else 1)  # non-zero exit on any failing question - what F20 gates a PR on


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

# F17: LLM-judge scoring for the three RAG-quality metrics the eval harness reports -
# faithfulness, answer relevancy, and context precision. The checklist names Ragas/DeepEval
# for this; both were evaluated and rejected for this repo specifically - `pip install ragas`
# here backtracks onto openai 3.3.1 -> 1.109.1 and langchain-openai 1.6.0 -> 1.1.9 to satisfy
# its pin range, a downgrade that would break every other engine sharing this venv (core/llm.py,
# engines/plain_rag_engine.py, engines/langgraph_engine.py all depend on the current versions).
# This scores the same three axes with the LLM already wired up via core.llm, using the same
# structured-output judging pattern LangGraph State Machine Engine (F13)'s route/verify nodes
# already use (`llm.with_structured_output(...)`) - no new dependency, no version conflict.
from pydantic import BaseModel, Field

FAITHFULNESS_THRESHOLD = 0.8
ANSWER_RELEVANCY_THRESHOLD = 0.8
CONTEXT_PRECISION_THRESHOLD = 0.6  # some retrieved-but-unused noise is tolerated; F10 re-ranking still narrows to top_k=3


class MetricJudgment(BaseModel):  # F17: one judge call's structured output
    score: float = Field(ge=0.0, le=1.0, description="0.0 = completely fails the metric, 1.0 = fully satisfies it")
    reasoning: str = Field(description="one or two sentences justifying the score")


class EvalScore(BaseModel):  # F17: one scored question, rolled up into a single pass/fail
    question: str
    answer: str
    faithfulness: MetricJudgment
    answer_relevancy: MetricJudgment
    context_precision: MetricJudgment

    @property
    def passed(self) -> bool:
        return (
            self.faithfulness.score >= FAITHFULNESS_THRESHOLD
            and self.answer_relevancy.score >= ANSWER_RELEVANCY_THRESHOLD
            and self.context_precision.score >= CONTEXT_PRECISION_THRESHOLD
        )


FAITHFULNESS_PROMPT = """You are grading a restaurant assistant's answer for FAITHFULNESS: does every claim in
the answer actually appear in, or follow directly from, the retrieved context below? An answer that adds a
detail not present in the context - a price, an ingredient, a policy - is unfaithful, even if that detail
happens to be true in general.

Retrieved context:
----------------
{context}
----------------
Answer to grade:
{answer}

Score 1.0 if every claim is grounded in the context, 0.0 if the answer invents something not in it, or a
value in between if only part of the answer is unsupported."""

ANSWER_RELEVANCY_PROMPT = """You are grading a restaurant assistant's answer for ANSWER RELEVANCY: does it
actually address what was asked, without padding, going off-topic, or answering a different question?

Question: {question}
Answer: {answer}

Score 1.0 if the answer directly and completely addresses the question, 0.0 if it doesn't address it at all,
or a value in between for a partial/tangential answer."""

CONTEXT_PRECISION_PROMPT = """You are grading a RAG system's retrieval for CONTEXT PRECISION: of the chunks
retrieved below, how many were actually useful for answering the question - as opposed to irrelevant chunks
that just added noise?

Question: {question}
Retrieved context:
----------------
{context}
----------------

Score 1.0 if every retrieved chunk was relevant and useful, 0.0 if none were, or a value in between for a
mix of useful and irrelevant chunks."""


def _judge(llm, prompt_template: str, **kwargs) -> MetricJudgment:
    return llm.with_structured_output(MetricJudgment).invoke(prompt_template.format(**kwargs))


def score_answer(llm, question: str, answer: str, context: str) -> tuple[MetricJudgment, MetricJudgment, MetricJudgment]:
    """F17: runs all three judge calls for one answered question, returning
    (faithfulness, answer_relevancy, context_precision)."""
    faithfulness = _judge(llm, FAITHFULNESS_PROMPT, context=context, answer=answer)
    answer_relevancy = _judge(llm, ANSWER_RELEVANCY_PROMPT, question=question, answer=answer)
    context_precision = _judge(llm, CONTEXT_PRECISION_PROMPT, question=question, context=context)
    return faithfulness, answer_relevancy, context_precision

F17:7 Line-by-Line Deep Dive: What evaluation/run_evals.py and evaluation/scoring.py Are Actually Doing

evaluation/scoring.py (full file at F17:6):

  • Lines 12–14 (thresholds) — FAITHFULNESS_THRESHOLD and ANSWER_RELEVANCY_THRESHOLD are both 0.8 (an answer either is or isn't grounded/relevant, so a high bar is cheap), while CONTEXT_PRECISION_THRESHOLD is 0.6 — deliberately looser, because Cross-Encoder Re-ranking (F10) already narrows retrieval to top_k=3 chunks and a single-fact question can still legitimately pull in a chunk that's mostly (but not entirely) relevant, as F17:4's Verification note found in the first real run.
  • Lines 17–19 (MetricJudgment) — score: float = Field(ge=0.0, le=1.0, ...) isn't just documentation: pydantic enforces that range on every judge response, so a judge call that somehow returns 1.5 or -0.2 raises a validation error immediately instead of silently corrupting a pass/fail decision downstream.
  • Lines 29–35 (EvalScore.passed) — a plain and across all three thresholds, not an average. An answer that's 1.0 faithful and 1.0 relevant but 0.4 on context precision still fails — averaging the three would let a strong faithfulness/relevancy score paper over genuinely bad retrieval, which defeats the point of measuring context precision separately in the first place.
  • Lines 38–73 (the three prompt templates) — each one grades a single axis in isolation: FAITHFULNESS_PROMPT never sees the original question (grounding either holds or it doesn't, independent of what was asked), ANSWER_RELEVANCY_PROMPT never sees the retrieved context (relevance is about the question/answer pair alone), and CONTEXT_PRECISION_PROMPT never sees the generated answer (it's grading retrieval, not generation). Keeping each judge blind to the inputs that don't belong to its axis is what keeps the three scores independent instead of all three quietly measuring the same thing.
  • Lines 76–77 (_judge) — llm.with_structured_output(MetricJudgment) is called fresh on every invocation rather than built once and reused; LangChain's structured-output wrapper is cheap to construct (it just binds a schema to the next call), so there's no caching to do here — unlike LangGraph State Machine Engine (F13)'s route/verify nodes, which bind their schemas once at graph-build time since those graphs are long-lived per cuisine.

evaluation/run_evals.py (full file at F17:5):

  • Line 29 (session_id) — one throwaway UUID session per run, not per question. It still doesn't matter for scoring, since line 37 always passes use_memory=False (see below) — but a single run-scoped id (versus a fresh one per question) keeps every question in one run traceable back to the same session in Observability & Tracing (F9)'s logs if something needs debugging.
  • Line 37 (use_memory=False) — the one deliberate divergence from how a real user's question would be answered. F8's hours questions bypass memory for the same reason menu_api.py's do; here every fixture question bypasses it, because a Dragon Roll question landing right after a corkage-fee question in the same eval run must not let Persistent Thread Checkpointing (F16)'s conversation history change what gets answered — a score regression has to mean "the system changed," never "the memory state this particular run happened to build up."
  • Line 39 (building context) — "\n\n".join(...) over source_documents reconstructs exactly the chunk boundaries CONTEXT_PRECISION_PROMPT grades against; the judge sees the same chunk-by-chunk shape the retriever actually returned; it's never handed one flattened blob that would hide how many separate chunks contributed.
  • Lines 66–72 (report's failure branch) — per-metric reasoning only prints for a failed question. Every metric's judge always returns a reasoning string, but only failures pay for the terminal noise of printing it — a full 15-question run's 4/5 passed style summary stays skimmable even though every judge call is producing an explanation under the hood.
  • Line 90 (sys.exit) — the only line in the file that talks to the process exit code rather than the console; everything above it is a plain function returning plain data, which is also exactly why run() and report() could be unit-tested directly in tests/test_evaluation.py without needing to spawn a subprocess and inspect its return code.

F17:8 Technical Deep Dive: Two Problems That Had Nothing to Do With the Scoring Logic

The scoring logic itself (three prompts, a pydantic schema, an and across three thresholds) went in cleanly. Both real problems building F17 showed up one layer down — in what it took to actually run the harness against live infrastructure, not in the harness's own code.

Problem 1: the checklist's named tool doesn't fit this repo's dependency graph. Ragas and DeepEval both implement faithfulness/answer-relevancy/context-precision directly — the obvious move was to install one and call it. pip install ragas --dry-run (checked before committing to either direction, not assumed) resolves to downgrading openai 3.3.1 → 1.109.1 and langchain-openai 1.6.0 → 1.1.9 to satisfy Ragas's own pinned range on langchain-community/datasets. Every engine in this repo (core/llm.py, engines/plain_rag_engine.py, engines/langgraph_engine.py) is built against the current, newer versions — a two-major-version openai downgrade to add an eval script would have been a strictly worse trade than writing three prompt templates by hand. evaluation/scoring.py's with_structured_output judges are the result — see F17:2's toolbox for the full reasoning.

Problem 2: a stale local cache silently broke retrieval before the harness could even run. The very first live run of python -m evaluation.run_evals failed before scoring a single question — get_engine("plain_rag") crashed inside core/vectorstore.py's module-level Ranker(model_name="ms-marco-MiniLM-L-12-v2") with onnxruntime.capi.onnxruntime_pybind11_state.NoSuchFile. Tracked down by hand: flashrank's Ranker._prepare_model_dir() only checks self.model_dir.exists() before deciding whether to (re-)download the model — it doesn't check whether the directory actually contains the .onnx file. An empty /tmp/ms-marco-MiniLM-L-12-v2/ directory left over from a previous interrupted download was enough to convince it the model was already cached, so every Ranker(...) call failed the same way, silently, with no download ever attempted. The fix was outside any of this repo's code: rmdir /tmp/ms-marco-MiniLM-L-12-v2 so the directory-exists check would actually fail and trigger a fresh download — confirmed by hand by re-running the harness immediately after and watching it download and load correctly. Worth flagging for anyone hitting the same NoSuchFile error locally: it means "empty cache directory," not "corrupt install."

Why this matters, in plain English: FAISS's semantic search is great at understanding meaning, but it can occasionally miss an exact keyword match (a specific dish name, say) if the phrasing doesn't line up well in vector space. Adding a classic keyword search alongside it, and blending the two rankings, means an exact match and a semantic match both get a fair shot at surfacing the right chunk.

Maps to checklist.csv day 18, "Hybrid Search (BM25 + FAISS)" — target location core/vectorstore.py.

What we'll build:

  • a BM25Retriever (keyword-based) running alongside the existing FAISS retriever
  • both combined via LangChain's EnsembleRetriever, with a tunable weighting between the two
  • feeds into the same Cross-Encoder Re-ranking (F10) step afterward — this adds a better candidate pool, it doesn't replace re-ranking
  • tracked via Mean Reciprocal Rank (MRR) and Context Recall, compared against FAISS alone

Status: Implemented. Every pull request now runs Unit Tests for Core Modules (F23)'s pytest suite, then Automated RAG Evals Harness (F17)'s real eval run, automatically — no one has to remember to run either by hand before merging, and a merge only stays blocked if a repository maintainer has separately turned on branch protection (see F20:3).

Maps to checklist.csv day 20, "CI/CD Eval Regression Gate" — target location .github/workflows/eval_gate.yml.

↑ Back to F20

F20:1 CI/CD Eval Regression Gate: Turning F17's Eval Suite From "Available" Into "Enforced"

Automated RAG Evals Harness (F17) already turns "did that change help or hurt?" into a number — but only for whoever remembers to type python -m evaluation.run_evals before merging. Nothing stops a pull request that quietly makes answers worse from being merged and shipped anyway, the same gap Unit Tests for Core Modules (F23) closed for the database/sheets/re-ranking modules but couldn't close for answer quality, since F23's suite mocks the LLM out entirely (see F23's own testing guide). CI/CD Eval Regression Gate closes that last gap: every pull request now runs both suites automatically, in GitHub's cloud, the moment it's opened or updated — no local step for a contributor to forget.

The Big Picture: Two Jobs, Chained

  • unit-tests — checks out the repo, installs requirements.txt, runs pytest (Unit Tests for Core Modules (F23)'s 48 tests). Fully mocked, no API key, no network — runs on every PR, including ones opened from a fork.
  • eval-gate — only starts once unit-tests finishes green (needs: unit-tests). Installs the same dependencies, then runs python -m evaluation.run_evals — Automated RAG Evals Harness (F17)'s real suite, a genuine embeddings + chat-completion round trip against OpenAI for all 15 fixture questions across all three cuisines. Skipped entirely on a fork's pull request, since GitHub never exposes this repo's OPENAI_API_KEY secret to a fork-triggered run (see F20:7).

Gating one job on the other isn't just cost-saving (real LLM calls cost real money and take real time — see F20:8) — it's a correctness call: if tests/test_evaluation.py is failing, the scoring logic itself (evaluation/scoring.py's thresholds, EvalScore.passed's all-three-must-pass rule) can't be trusted, so a green eval run wouldn't mean anything yet.

What Each Job Actually Runs

  • actions/checkout@v4 — clones the PR's branch onto the runner
  • actions/setup-python@v5 (python-version: "3.11", matching the local venv/pyvenv.cfg) with cache: pip — caches requirements.txt's resolved wheels between runs so repeat PRs don't redownload FAISS/flashrank/langchain from scratch every time
  • pip install -r requirements.txt — the exact same dependency set every engine (Modular Engine Strategy Factory (F12), LangGraph State Machine Engine (F13)) already runs against locally, not a CI-only subset
  • pytest / python -m evaluation.run_evals — the same two commands F23's and F17's own Testing Guides already tell a human to run by hand; the workflow doesn't reimplement either, it just automates invoking them

For the full, step-by-step workflow definition, please refer to the GitHub Repository & Code Details link.

Tags: CI/CD, GitHub Actions, Quality Gate, F20

Tools & Libraries (per checklist.csv's "Primary Tools & Libraries" for #20):
  • GitHub Actions — used, as .github/workflows/eval_gate.yml — no separate CI product evaluated or needed, since the repo is already hosted on GitHub.
  • pytest — used, exactly as Unit Tests for Core Modules (F23) already runs it locally — the unit-tests job, no new configuration beyond installing it.
  • Ragas CLI — not used, for the same reason Automated RAG Evals Harness (F17) didn't add the ragas package in the first place: it backtracks this repo's openai/langchain-openai pins hard enough to break every engine sharing the venv — see F17:2's toolbox and F17:8 for the confirmed dependency resolution. F20 gates on evaluation/run_evals.py's exit code instead, which is already shaped like a CLI's pass/fail exit code without needing a CLI.

F20:2 Architecture Summary: One New File, Nothing Else Touched

No production code changed to make this possible — evaluation/run_evals.py's main() (F17) already exits 0 on an all-pass run and 1 otherwise, and pytest's exit code needs no extra wiring at all. GitHub Actions already treats a non-zero exit code from any run: step as a failed job, and a failed job as a failed check on the PR — the entire gate is one YAML file describing which commands to run and in what order, not new application logic.

  • .github/workflows/eval_gate.yml — the only new file. Two jobs (unit-tests, eval-gate), triggered on pull_request targeting main and on workflow_dispatch (a manual "Run workflow" button in GitHub's UI, for checking the gate without opening a PR).

Why eval-gate Is Conditioned On the PR's Source Repo

if: github.event.pull_request.head.repo.full_name == github.repository || github.event_name == 'workflow_dispatch' — GitHub Actions never hands a base repository's secrets to a workflow run triggered by a fork's pull request (a deliberate GitHub security boundary, not a choice made here); without this guard, eval-gate would still attempt to run on a fork PR, find OPENAI_API_KEY empty, and fail every fork contribution's check for a reason that has nothing to do with their change. The condition lets unit-tests — which needs no secret — still run and gate every PR including fork ones, while eval-gate only runs where the secret is actually available: same-repo branches, and manual workflow_dispatch runs (always triggered from within the repo, never from a fork).

F20:3 Integration Guide: What Actually Got Touched

  • .github/workflows/eval_gate.yml (new) — the workflow itself, see F20:5 for the full file.
  • evaluation/run_evals.py, evaluation/scoring.py, tests/ — read, not modified. The gate calls the exact commands Automated RAG Evals Harness (F17) and Unit Tests for Core Modules (F23) already defined; nothing about either suite needed to change to become CI-runnable.
  • requirements.txt — unchanged. No new dependency: pytest was already in it (F23), and the eval harness reuses what F17 already installed.

One-Time Setup This Repo Still Needs, Outside the Codebase

A workflow file alone doesn't fully activate the gate — two settings live in GitHub's UI, not in git, so they survive independently of any commit:

  • Add the OPENAI_API_KEY repository secret — Settings → Secrets and variables → Actions → New repository secret, same key name the local .env file already uses in core/llm.py's build_llm_and_embeddings(). Without it, eval-gate runs and fails immediately on the same RuntimeError("Set OPENAI_API_KEY or AZURE_OPENAI_API_KEY...") a local run would raise with no .env present — not a bug in the workflow, just the secret not being set yet.
  • Turn on branch protection for main — Settings → Branches → add a rule requiring the unit-tests and eval-gate status checks to pass before merging. Until this is turned on, the workflow still runs and still reports a red/green check on every PR, but a red check is purely informational — it doesn't block the "Merge pull request" button. This is the one part of F20 that genuinely can't be committed as a file; it's a one-time click-through (or a one-time gh api call) a repository maintainer does once.

F20:4 Testing Guide: How to Verify CI/CD Eval Regression Gate (F20)

1) Prove the underlying commands pass locally first — the exact two commands the workflow runs, in the exact order it runs them:

source venv/bin/activate
pytest                          # unit-tests job
python -m evaluation.run_evals  # eval-gate job (needs OPENAI_API_KEY in .env)

A real local run of the first command: 48 passed, 1 warning in 0.99s — all of Unit Tests for Core Modules (F23)'s suite, unchanged by anything F20 adds. The second command's real output is already captured in Automated RAG Evals Harness (F17)'s own Testing Guide (F17:4) — F20:6 below reproduces the relevant lines in the context of what shows up in the Actions log specifically.

2) Validate the workflow file itself without pushing — YAML syntax and GitHub's own schema, both checkable before ever opening a PR:

python3 -c "import yaml; yaml.safe_load(open('.github/workflows/eval_gate.yml'))"  # parses clean

3) See it actually gate a PR — push a branch, open a pull request against main, and the "Checks" section on the PR shows both jobs running automatically: unit-tests first, then eval-gate once it's green. A workflow_dispatch run (Actions tab → "Eval Regression Gate" → "Run workflow") exercises the exact same two jobs without needing an open PR at all — useful for checking the gate still works after a dependency bump, independent of any specific change under review.

Verification: ran pytest locally (the exact command unit-tests runs) — 48 passed, 1 warning in 0.99s, confirming the job's only step succeeds against this repo's current state. eval_gate.yml parses clean with yaml.safe_load. The eval-gate job's own command (python -m evaluation.run_evals) was already verified live, against all three cuisines' real menus, in Automated RAG Evals Harness (F17)'s own Testing Guide — F20 doesn't change that command, only automates calling it, so that verification carries over rather than needing to be re-spent here. What hasn't been exercised yet from inside this session: an actual GitHub-hosted run, since that needs the OPENAI_API_KEY repository secret and branch protection set up in GitHub's UI first (F20:3) — a one-time step for whoever administers this repository on GitHub.

# F20: CI/CD Eval Regression Gate.
#
# Two jobs, chained:
#   1. unit-tests - the F23 pytest suite (tests/). Fully mocked, no API key, no network.
#      Runs on every PR, including ones from forks.
#   2. eval-gate  - only after unit-tests passes. Runs the F17 harness
#      (`python -m evaluation.run_evals`) against real ground-truth fixtures through a real
#      OpenAI call, and fails the build if any question drops below scoring.py's thresholds.
#      Skipped on fork PRs, which don't have access to this repo's OPENAI_API_KEY secret -
#      GitHub Actions never exposes a base repo's secrets to a workflow run triggered by a
#      fork's pull request.
name: Eval Regression Gate

on:
  pull_request:
    branches: [main]
  workflow_dispatch: {} # manual "Run workflow" button, for checking the gate without opening a PR

jobs:
  unit-tests: # F23
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-python@v5
        with:
          python-version: "3.11"
          cache: pip
          cache-dependency-path: requirements.txt
      - run: pip install -r requirements.txt
      - run: pytest

  eval-gate: # F17, gated on F23 passing first - a broken unit means the eval numbers can't be trusted either
    needs: unit-tests
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    if: github.event.pull_request.head.repo.full_name == github.repository || github.event_name == 'workflow_dispatch'
    env:
      OPENAI_API_KEY: ${{ secrets.OPENAI_API_KEY }}
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-python@v5
        with:
          python-version: "3.11"
          cache: pip
          cache-dependency-path: requirements.txt
      - run: pip install -r requirements.txt
      # menus/*.pdf are checked in; vectorstores/ is gitignored, so this build is a fresh
      # FAISS index from PDF on every run - see core/vectorstore.py's get_retriever().
      - run: python -m evaluation.run_evals

F20:6 What a Real Gate Run Looks Like

The unit-tests job — a real local run of the exact command it executes:

$ pytest -q
................................................                         [100%]
48 passed, 1 warning in 0.99s

The eval-gate job — its one step is python -m evaluation.run_evals, the identical command whose real output against the live plain_rag engine and the real sushi menu is already shown in full in Automated RAG Evals Harness (F17)'s Testing Guide (F17:4). The shape that matters for this gate specifically is the last line of that output:

4/5 passed

and the process exit code behind it — sys.exit(0 if all_passed else 1) in evaluation/run_evals.py's main(). A 4/5 result exits 1, which GitHub Actions reports as a failed step, which marks the eval-gate job — and therefore the PR's "Eval Regression Gate" check — red. Nothing about F20 changes what F17 scores or how; F20's only contribution is turning that exit code into a check on a pull request instead of a number a person has to remember to look at.

F20:7 Line-by-Line Deep Dive: What eval_gate.yml Is Actually Doing

.github/workflows/eval_gate.yml (full file at F20:5):

  • Lines 13–15 (on:) — pull_request: branches: [main] scopes the trigger to PRs targeting main, not every push to every branch; pushing commits to an open PR re-triggers the same two jobs automatically, which is what makes this a true gate rather than a one-time check at PR open. workflow_dispatch: {} is a second, independent trigger — an empty input set, since this gate needs no parameters to run the same thing a PR run would.
  • Line 24 (cache: pip) — keys the cache off cache-dependency-path: requirements.txt, so a run only redownloads FAISS/flashrank/langchain's wheels when that file's contents actually change, not on every single PR — the same install-once-reuse-often shape core/vectorstore.py's get_retriever() already applies to the FAISS index itself (F12), just at the dependency-install layer instead of the data layer.
  • Line 33 (needs: unit-tests) — the only line establishing the two jobs' order; without it, GitHub Actions would run both jobs in parallel by default, which would let a real OpenAI bill get spent scoring answers from a build whose own unit tests are broken.
  • Line 35 (if:) — evaluated once, before the job's runner is even provisioned; if it resolves false the job shows as "skipped" (not "failed") on the PR, which matters for branch protection — a required check that's skipped for a structural reason (fork PR) doesn't behave the same as one that ran and failed. See F20:2 for why this condition exists at all.
  • Lines 36–37 (env: OPENAI_API_KEY) — set at the job level, not the step level, so every step in eval-gate (not just the final run) has it available; in practice only the last step reads it, but scoping it to the job rather than one step keeps it available if a future step (a cache warm, a smoke-test call) needed it too, without having to duplicate the line.
  • Line 45 (the vectorstores comment) — documents, not enforces: vectorstores/ is in .gitignore (Test the chunking (RAG & Vectorstore) (F3)), so every single eval-gate run rebuilds all three cuisines' FAISS indexes from menus/*.pdf from scratch — there's no persisted-index cache step in this workflow, unlike the pip cache two lines above. See F20:8 for why that's a deliberate omission, not an oversight.

F20:8 Technical Deep Dive: What This Gate Costs, and What It Deliberately Doesn't Guarantee

This gate spends real money on every PR update, on purpose. Unlike unit-tests, eval-gate is not free or instant: python -m evaluation.run_evals makes one embeddings call plus one chat-completion call per fixture question against the live engine (15 questions), plus three more judge chat-completion calls per question (Automated RAG Evals Harness (F17)'s faithfulness / answer-relevancy / context-precision), and rebuilds three FAISS indexes from PDF from a cold cache every time (see F20:7's last bullet) — roughly 75 LLM calls and a minute or two of runner time per push to an open PR. That's the direct, accepted cost of the thing F20 actually buys: an answer-quality regression gets caught by a machine on the PR itself, instead of by a person noticing a worse answer after it's already merged. Caching the FAISS indexes between runs (an actions/cache step keyed on the PDFs' hash, mirroring the pip cache already in the workflow) would cut the rebuild cost but not the ~60 judge/answer LLM calls, which is where nearly all of the per-run cost actually is — left as a follow-up rather than built speculatively here, the same "don't build for a hypothetical" call Modular Engine Strategy Factory (F12) made about skipping a formal Abstract Factory class for one engine.

A red check is not the same as a blocked merge — and that's a GitHub platform boundary, not a gap in this workflow. As F20:3 covers, nothing in eval_gate.yml itself can force a merge to wait; GitHub Actions' only lever is reporting a pass/fail status back to the PR, and whether that status actually blocks the merge button is a separate, UI-configured branch-protection rule scoped to the whole repository, not to this one workflow file. A workflow can't enable branch protection on itself — that would mean a file inside the repo controlling a permission boundary around the repo, which GitHub deliberately keeps outside of what any committed file can touch. Practically: this file alone gets you visibility (a red X shows up); a maintainer's one-time settings change gets you enforcement (a red X blocks merging).

Non-determinism is inherited, not introduced. evaluation/scoring.py's judge LLM calls are graded by another LLM call, and core/llm.py's ChatOpenAI(temperature=0) makes that "best-effort deterministic," not guaranteed — the same caveat core/llm.py's own comment block already notes about seed=42 not being fully guaranteed either. In practice this means a PR that changed nothing relevant to answer quality could, rarely, flip a borderline context_precision score across its 0.6 threshold between two runs of the identical code — a flaky-test failure mode this gate shares with any LLM-judged CI check, not something F20's own YAML introduces or could fix by itself.

F23:1 Unit Tests for Core Modules: Testing the Logic, Not the Vibes

Every feature so far has been verified the same two ways: run it and read the answer by eye (the pattern Automated RAG Evals Harness (F17) is meant to eventually replace for answer quality), or exercise it through a real HTTP request, as LangGraph State Machine Engine (F13)'s Verification note describes. Neither approach touches the plain Python functions underneath — core/sheets.py's date-phrase parser, core/database.py's SQL aggregation, core/vectorstore.py's re-ranking — in isolation. A bug in "does 'the day after tomorrow' beat the 'tomorrow' substring check" doesn't need an LLM call, a FAISS index, or a live Google Sheet to catch; it needs a function call and an assertion.

F23 is a pytest suite that does exactly that: import the function, call it with a known input, assert the known-correct output — no network, no API key, no model weights on disk. The three modules it covers are the ones with the most non-obvious branching logic and the least LLM involvement: resolve_target_days()'s relative-date parsing, get_session_totals()'s SQL aggregation, and rerank_documents()'s cross-encoder re-scoring.

How to Run It

No .env, no API key, no running server — just the venv and pytest:

source venv/bin/activate
pip install -r requirements.txt   # pulls in pytest
pytest tests/ -v

That runs all 41 tests and finishes in well under a second, since nothing here waits on a network call, a model load, or a real database file. Narrower runs while iterating on one module:

pytest tests/test_sheets.py -v        # just core/sheets.py's tests
pytest -k "weekend or tomorrow" -v    # just the tests whose name matches

What's Actually Tested, File by File

tests/test_database.py (6 tests) — core/database.py's SQLite persistence, each run against a throwaway tmp_path database, never the project's real usage.db:

  • test_init_db_creates_usage_log_table — init_db() actually creates the usage_log table
  • test_init_db_is_idempotent — calling init_db() twice doesn't raise on the already-existing table
  • test_get_session_totals_for_unknown_session_returns_zeros_not_error — a session with zero logged calls gets back all-zero totals, not a SQL None or an exception
  • test_log_call_persists_a_row — log_call() writes exactly the values it was given, read back with a raw SELECT
  • test_get_session_totals_sums_multiple_calls_in_same_session — two logged calls in one session sum correctly across all four tracked columns
  • test_get_session_totals_does_not_leak_across_sessions — a second session's usage never bleeds into the first session's totals

tests/test_sheets.py (30 tests) — core/sheets.py's date parsing, intent routing, and Sheets lookups, with date.today() frozen to a fixed Thursday and every gspread call monkeypatched:

  • resolve_target_days (9 tests) — defaults to today when nothing matches, "tomorrow", "the day after tomorrow" (proving the substring-collision guard beats a naive "tomorrow" in q check), "in 3 days", "5 days from now", "this weekend" (returns both Saturday and Sunday), a named weekday ahead of today, a named weekday that is today (must resolve to today, not +7 days), and an abbreviated weekday ("fri")
  • detect_ops_intent (6 tests) — a 5-case parametrized check ("specials" keyword → "specials", "open"/"close"/"holiday" → "hours", nothing → None), plus one dedicated test proving specials keywords win when both fire on the same question ("any specials during holiday hours?")
  • _is_active (8 parametrized cases) — every truthy spelling the sheet might actually contain ("True" / "YES" / "y" / "1" / " active ") reads as active; "False" / "no" / "" don't
  • get_daily_specials (2 tests) — inactive rows get filtered out; a day filter keeps that day's rows and "All Week" rows together
  • get_hours_and_events (2 tests) — filters down to one matching row when a target date is given; returns every row when it isn't
  • _open_tab (3 parametrized cases) — SpreadsheetNotFound, WorksheetNotFound, and APIError (built with a fake response object, since gspread's own APIError.__init__ reads response.json()) all get wrapped into a plain RuntimeError, matching what the rest of the app already expects to catch

tests/test_vectorstore.py (5 tests) — core/vectorstore.py's re-ranking, with flashrank.Ranker faked out before import (see F23:8 for why):

  • test_rerank_documents_returns_empty_list_unchanged — an empty document list short-circuits without ever calling the ranker
  • test_rerank_documents_reorders_by_ranker_score — a scripted, out-of-order ranker response actually reorders the real Document objects to match, not just returns something
  • test_rerank_documents_respects_top_k — asking for top_k=1 truncates to exactly the single top-scored document
  • test_wrap_with_reranking_builds_retriever_with_given_top_k — the wrapper actually stores the base retriever and top_k it was constructed with
  • test_reranking_retriever_reranks_base_retriever_results — end-to-end: the query string reaches both the base retriever and the re-ranking step unchanged

The Big Picture: One Test File Per Module, External Calls Mocked at the Boundary

Three test files, each targeting one core/*.py module, all following the same shape: real logic runs unmodified, only the thing outside the process (a database file, a Google Sheets API call, an ONNX model load) gets swapped for a fake:

  • tests/test_database.py — core/database.py against a real SQLite file, but a throwaway one (pytest's built-in tmp_path fixture), never the project's actual usage.db
  • tests/test_sheets.py — core/sheets.py with _open_tab() and _get_client() monkeypatched to fakes that return canned rows instead of calling gspread, and date.today() frozen to a fixed Thursday so relative-date assertions ("tomorrow", "this weekend") don't depend on what day the suite happens to run
  • tests/test_vectorstore.py — core/vectorstore.py with flashrank.Ranker swapped into sys.modules for a mock before the module is first imported — see F23:8 for why that has to happen before import, not after

What's Imported (and Why)

  • pytest (new, added to requirements.txt) — the runner, plus its tmp_path and monkeypatch fixtures, which cover every mocking need here without a single explicit unittest.mock.patch decorator
  • unittest.mock.MagicMock (Python standard library) — used directly only where a fixture return value needs to be an inspectable stand-in (a fake cross-encoder ranker, a fake run manager), not a monkeypatched attribute
  • gspread.exceptions (already a dependency, via F8) — imported in the test file itself, so the error-wrapping tests raise the exact exception classes core/sheets.py's _open_tab() actually catches, not a generic stand-in

For the full, step-by-step code implementation, please refer to the GitHub Repository & Code Details link.

Tags: Testing, pytest, unittest.mock, Test Coverage, F23

F23:2 Architecture Summary: Three Files, Mirroring the Three Modules Under Test

No production code changed to make this possible — every module under test already exposed plain, importable functions that take their dependencies as arguments (db_path, day, top_k, ...), so nothing needed a seam added to become testable. The suite's only structural pieces:

  • tests/conftest.py — inserts the project root onto sys.path, so import core.sheets resolves the same way regardless of which directory pytest is invoked from
  • one test file per module — test_database.py, test_sheets.py, test_vectorstore.py — deliberately not the checklist's single test_core.py. Each module needed a different kind of isolation (a temp file, a frozen clock, a faked import); splitting them keeps each file's fixtures scoped to the one module they actually apply to, instead of a grab-bag of unrelated fixtures living in one flat file
  • no shared fixtures beyond the path fix — conftest.py stays a single sys.path line; each file's mocking setup lives with the tests that need it

F23:3 Integration Guide: What Actually Got Touched

  • tests/ (new directory) — conftest.py, test_database.py, test_sheets.py, test_vectorstore.py. Nothing outside tests/ was created.
  • requirements.txt — added pytest. No other new dependency; unittest.mock is standard library.
  • core/database.py, core/sheets.py, core/vectorstore.py — read, not modified.

F23:4 Testing Guide: How to test Unit Tests for Core Modules (F23)

1) Install and run the whole suite — no .env, no API key, no running server:

source venv/bin/activate
pip install -r requirements.txt
pytest tests/ -v

Expect 41 passed in well under a second — the suite touches nothing outside the process (a throwaway SQLite file, mocked gspread/flashrank calls).

2) Run just one module's tests, while iterating on it:

pytest tests/test_sheets.py -v

3) Run a single test by name (useful once the suite grows past a skim-the-output size):

pytest -k "weekend" -v

4) Prove a test actually catches something — the acceptance check for any new test, not just F23's: temporarily break the code it covers (e.g. flip resolve_target_days's "weekend" branch to return only Saturday) and confirm the matching test fails, then revert. Every test in this suite was checked this way before being counted as done.

F23:7 Line-by-Line Deep Dive: What tests/test_vectorstore.py Is Actually Doing

  • Lines 17–30 (vectorstore fixture) — builds a fake flashrank module (ModuleType("flashrank")) with a mocked Ranker class, installs it into sys.modules via monkeypatch.setitem, evicts any already-imported core.vectorstore from sys.modules, then imports it fresh. Only after all of that does core/vectorstore.py's module-level _ranker = Ranker(...) line run — against the fake, never the real ONNX model loader.
  • Lines 37–47 (FakeRetriever) — a real BaseRetriever subclass, not a MagicMock. See F23:8 for why a mock doesn't work here.
  • Lines 50–52 — the empty-list short-circuit: asserts both the return value and that _ranker.rerank was never called, so the test would fail if someone "optimized" the empty-list guard away and the code started calling the ranker with zero passages.
  • Lines 55–66 — the core re-ranking behavior: feeds a scripted, out-of-order rerank() return value in and asserts rerank_documents() reorders the actual Document objects to match, not just that it returns something.
  • Lines 92–111 — RerankingRetriever._get_relevant_documents() exercised end-to-end through a fake base retriever and a monkeypatched rerank_documents, confirming the query string reaches both the base retriever and the re-ranking step unchanged.

F23:8 Technical Deep Dive: Two Mocking Problems the Checklist Didn't Mention

The checklist names unittest.mock as the tool and tests/test_core.py as the target, but building this surfaced two problems a single flat test file and a plain Mock() don't solve.

Problem 1: core/vectorstore.py loads a real model at import time. _ranker = Ranker(model_name="ms-marco-MiniLM-L-12-v2") runs the moment the module is imported, not when a function is called — so patching core.vectorstore._ranker after import is already too late; the real onnxruntime.InferenceSession load has already happened (confirmed by hand: it fails outright with an onnxruntime.capi.onnxruntime_pybind11_state.NoSuchFile error when the model isn't already cached on disk). The fix is the vectorstore fixture in F23:5 — install a fake flashrank module into sys.modules before core.vectorstore is imported for the first time, and evict any cached import so the fixture's fake is guaranteed to be what Ranker(...) resolves to.

Problem 2: RerankingRetriever rejects a bare MagicMock. It's a pydantic model (via LangChain's BaseRetriever) with base_retriever: BaseRetriever as a typed field — pydantic validates that on construction, and a MagicMock isn't an instance of BaseRetriever, so wrap_with_reranking(MagicMock(), ...) raises a pydantic_core.ValidationError before the test even gets to the assertion (confirmed by hand, not assumed). The fix is FakeRetriever — a minimal real BaseRetriever subclass that records calls into a plain list instead of a mock's call history, satisfying pydantic's type check while still being inspectable.

Both problems are the same shape: a library's own type checking or import-time behavior gets in the way of the "just mock it" default, and the fix is to mock at the actual boundary (the module registry, a real base class) instead of the first object that happens to be nearby.

  • every external dependency mocked at the boundary — a temp SQLite file, a fake gspread worksheet, a fake flashrank module installed before import — so the whole suite runs offline in well under a second

  • zero changes to any production file — every module under test was already structured to accept its dependencies as arguments
